articles.title: Amazon seemingly leaked Jason Statham’s entire Mutiny movie
articles.summary: The film isn’t supposed to hit theaters for two days, but it was briefly available to stream on Prime Video.
articles.body: Jason Statham’s upcoming film Mutiny is set to hit theaters on August 21st, but for at least an hour today it was available to stream in full on the US version of Amazon Prime Video. My colleague Dominic Preston was able to verify that all 1 hour and 35 minutes of the movie was available to watch on Amazon’s streaming platform, though it now shows as “unavailable.” The Mutiny website and marketing materials state that it’ll only be available in theaters when it’s officially released in two days. There’s nothing to suggest that this was released on Prime Video intentionally, or that it’s intended to be some marketing stunt — neither the Punch Palace Productions and MadRiver Pictures production studios, nor US distributor Lionsgate, are owned by Amazon. We have reached out to Amazon for comment. It’s unclear when Mutiny was added to Prime Video US. The Prime Video listing is fully populated with the cast list, video thumbnail, and a blurb that reads: “After his billionaire industrialist boss is murdered in front of him, Cole Reed is set up to take the fall for the crime — leaving him on the run as he works to uncover a conspiracy.” [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FKSdXH89jbo&list=PLJ7A97yl9oXphnKstrll_GetLGHMNodCn&index=1] Update, August 19th: The film is no longer available to stream.

articles.title: Why soccer fans are sliding into Olivia Rodrigo's Instagram comments
articles.summary: The pop star’s account has been infiltrated by fans of FC Barcelona after the signing of Rodri, a Spanish midfielder who has publicly shunned social media.
articles.body:
Two weeks ago, Olivia Rodrigo posted photos to Instagram of herself at Lollapalooza in Chicago, where she joined the Smashing Pumpkins for a surprise performance of "Thirty-Three."

In one shot, she appeared to be backstage holding a cup of tea. In the other, she was onstage alongside frontman Billy Corgan.

"Olivia + Smashing Pumpkins was the crossover I never knew I needed," one fan wrote in the comments section.

"My favorite band and my favorite modern pop artist in one," wrote another.

But the comments about the unlikely collaboration were soon infiltrated by fans of FC Barcelona, which earlier this week announced the signing of Rodri, a Spanish midfielder and winner of the 2026 World Cup Golden Ball as the best player in this year's final.

"Welcome to Barça Rodri 💙♥️" one commenter wrote.

"I know you are not Rodri, but welcome to Barca anyways," wrote another.

So why are Barça fans using Rodrigo's Instagram account to welcome Rodri (full name: Rodrigo Hernández Cascante) to the team?

There are a few reasons. Rodri, who most recently played for Manchester City, doesn't have a public Instagram account, which was evident in 2024, when he won the Ballon d'Or for best soccer player.

Real Madrid fans who were upset that Rodri won the award — and not Vinícius Júnior — also flooded Rodrigo's Instagram account, saying he was undeserving of the annual honor. (As Marca reports , Argentine soccer player Rodrigo De Paul was also sent comments intended for his similarly named peer.)

Real Madrid fans are abusing Olivia Rodrigo on Instagram thinking that she is Rodri 😭 pic.twitter.com/aKcrPwbM0Y — Footy Humour (@FootyHumour) October 29, 2024

Real Madrid fans are abusing Olivia Rodrigo on Instagram thinking that she is Rodri 😭 pic.twitter.com/aKcrPwbM0Y

— Footy Humour (@FootyHumour) October 29, 2024

Some commenters say the new round of Barça-related comments has less to do with mistaken identity and more about riffing on the 2024 Real Madrid hijinks.

While she's not, in fact, Rodri, Rodrigo does have ties to FC Barcelona.

Culers, Olivia Rodrigo has a message for you! 💬 @spotify @oliviarodrigo 🩷 pic.twitter.com/WFrqUG8ppB — FC Barcelona (@FCBarcelona) May 10, 2026

Culers, Olivia Rodrigo has a message for you! 💬 @spotify @oliviarodrigo 🩷 pic.twitter.com/WFrqUG8ppB

— FC Barcelona (@FCBarcelona) May 10, 2026

The club released a special limited-edition jersey with Rodrigo's initials last season as part of a sponsorship with Spotify.

And earlier this year, she wished Barcelona luck ahead of its rival match, El Clásico, against Real Madrid — which Rodrigo attended .

articles.title: New movies to watch this weekend: See 'Insidious: Out of the Further' in theaters, rent 'Toy Story 5,' stream 'The Christophers' on Hulu
articles.summary: The Anthony Bourdain biopic "Tony" and Matthew McConaughey's indie gem "The Rivals of Amziah King" also expand nationwide — and both are worth watching.
articles.body:
Welcome to Trust Me, I Watch Everything , a weekly guide to all the new movies out each Friday.

This week's buzziest release is the sixth entry in the Insidious horror franchise, Insidious: Out of the Further, which takes things in an exciting new direction. The latest film from Jane Schoenbrun, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, also expands nationwide, as does the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony and Matthew McConaughey's outstanding The Rivals of Amziah King .

If you'd rather stay home, you can now rent or buy Toy Story 5, one of the biggest box-office hits of the year.

Want to stick to a streaming service you're likely already paying for? Steven Soderbergh's The Christophers is well worth a watch on Hulu, and the jump-scare fest Passenger makes its way to Paramount+.

Movies newly available on streaming services you may already have

The biggest release : Insidious: Out of the Further

Why I liked it: Insidious: Out of the Further has to be one of the most inspired sixth entries in a franchise that I can think of, especially when you consider that it likely only exists because 2023's Insidious: The Red Door was such a hit, despite being the weakest entry.

That film closed the, uh, red door on the Lambert family's story, so in Out of the Further, we're introduced to a new family and a bevy of spooky new ghouls. Gemma, a young mother raising her daughter in the house she grew up in, discovers that not only can she travel into the Further, but she also possesses a very special ability: She can bring what lives in the Further back to the real world. It's a fun, goofy twist that brings a whole new dimension to the proceedings (pun intended).

Despite ultimately functioning as a metaphor for trauma — a modern horror trope so prevalent it's barely worth mentioning at this point, just assume it's the case — the movie works because it's both scary and silly. The jump scares are incredibly effective, and the entities from the Further are unsettling and/or gross to varying degrees. It's so earnestly committed to the movie's world and its random rules that it's easy to get wrapped up in it all.

The horror set pieces are truly excellent, including a standout sequence involving a pillow fort and endless couch cushions that brings Backrooms to mind, and another one involving the grossest visit to the dentist you'll likely ever experience. (Hopefully, at least.)

It leans into the ridiculousness in the back half in a way that may lose some audience members, but really won me over. It's visually inventive throughout, especially when the characters jump back and forth between the Further and reality. The childhood trauma stuff, despite earning a perfunctory eye roll from me up top, is actually well-established and unexpectedly satisfying on a narrative level by the end. They earned it!

It's still so fun that scream queen Lin Shaye, 82, is a genuine movie star, and she's well-deployed here, tethering this entry to the others in a fun way. Also, her annoying sidekicks are nowhere to be found, which is a plus, as far as I'm concerned.

Why I liked it: Toy Story 5 continues the storied franchise's tradition of laughs, tears and, frankly, just being damn good movies that both kids and adults can enjoy.

When Bonnie receives a Lilypad tablet as a gift and becomes obsessed, Buzz, Woody, Jessie and the rest of the gang have to go head-to-head with the all-new threat to playtime.

Why I liked it: Steven Soderbergh's latest film sees the prolific filmmaker dropping all pretense and making the "it's about making art!" element the text instead of the subtext. How to watch: The Christophers is now streaming on Hulu .

Why I liked it: Passenger is an extremely silly horror movie that nevertheless does exactly what it says on the tin and delivers the scary goods.

After a young couple witnesses a gruesome highway accident, they soon realize they did not leave the crash scene alone. A demonic presence that won't stop until it claims them both turns their #VanLife adventure into a nightmare. In short, it's a haunted house movie, but set in a van.

The opening scene, in particular, is incredibly effective at setting the stage for what follows; I was most impressed by how casually funny it was right off the bat, making you laugh immediately with characters you've only just met. The scene that unfolds is tense, and the cut-to-title had the crowd I saw it with screaming with delight.

You'll be checking your watch, however, any time the movie slows down to let the characters talk about their inner lives. It's not the kind of movie that requires much relationship backstory, and whenever the boyfriend gets earnest about his ambitions for his van, it's hard not to laugh at how thinly drawn they are. But all the spooky set pieces are well-constructed enough and will make you jump, so it's worth enduring the boring bits.

Norwegian filmmaker André Øvredal has yet to top his debut feature, The Autopsy of Jane Doe, but Passenger is his most fun work since that truly great horror film, after the duds The Last Voyage of the Demeter , Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark and Umma, which nobody saw.

It's easier to experience it than describe it. Now streaming on Shudder.

The film follows the true story of John Davidson's journey from a misunderstood teenager in 1980s Britain to a present-day advocate for the understanding and acceptance of Tourette's syndrome. The film follows the true story of John Davidson's journey from a misunderstood teenager in 1980s Britain to a present-day advocate for the understanding and acceptance of Tourette's syndrome. Now streaming on Netflix .

articles.title: We’re All Going to the World’s Fair is an intimate coming-of-age horror film
articles.summary: Now is the perfect time to revisit Jane Schoenbrun’s first film, We’re All Going to the World’s Fair, an intimate coming-of-age horror film like nothing else.
articles.body: Jane Schoenbrun’s latest film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, is making a splash in theaters right now. So it seems like the perfect time to revisit their first film, We’re All Going to the World’s Fair. I fell in love with this film when I first saw it at Sundance in 2021.  We are immediately introduced to our protagonist, Casey, as she engages in the World’s Fair Challenge, a sort of ARG creepypasta meets ice bucket challenge. There’s a creepy mantra, some bloodletting, and a mysterious video — basically a speedrun of horror movie tropes. But having them all delivered by this young girl alone in her room who just stares directly into her webcam the whole time is unsettling. And I actually physically recoiled when she jabbed herself repeatedly with a pin to draw blood. [Media: https://youtu.be/y0AnGfzgh_w] The idea is that people perform the ritual and then they’re supposed to change in some sort of nebulous way. It’s set up as some sort of “game” where people are supposed to report their symptoms, as they turn into plastic or their guts and become Tetris pieces. Ultimately, World’s Fair is a coming-of-age story about a lonely young girl. She’s never shown talking to kids her own age. Her father is never seen, only heard, and does nothing but yell. She desperately attempts to connect with others by uploading videos documenting the changes she experiences after performing the challenge.  Importantly, unlike many other coming-of-age films, World’s Fair isn’t about Casey’s sexual awakening and avoids sexualizing her entirely. Instead, it’s about her search for belonging in an extremely online world. Basically the only other character to get any screen time is JLB, a lonely middle-aged man who claims Casey is in danger. The relationship between JLB and Casey adds another layer of unease to the film, which already blends horror elements with uncomfortably intimate glimpses into the life of a young girl. The whole thing has a voyeuristic quality. It’s never explicitly stated, but it certainly seems like JLB is attempting to groom the vulnerable Casey. The movie stews in its uncomfortable ambiguity. And that’s part of what makes it great. It may not reach the surreal or campy heights of I Saw the TV Glow or Camp Miasma, but it’s a rare indie cinema original that uses body horror tropes in new and interesting ways. We’re All Going to the World’s Fair is available to stream on Criterion Channel, Kanopy, and Hoopla.

articles.title: Motown songwriter behind 'Money (That's What I Want)' and other hits dead at 87
articles.summary: Janie Bradford Hobbs co-wrote "Money (That's What I Want)" with Berry Gordy and penned hits for Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder and The Supremes.
articles.body: Janie Bradford Hobbs, an early Motown songwriter who co-wrote "Money (That’s What I Want)" and penned songs recorded by Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder and other music legends, has died after an extended illness at 87. Bradford Hobbs died at a Los Angeles hospital, her family said Saturday. Born in Charleston, Missouri, Bradford Hobbs later moved to Detroit, where neighbor and singer Jackie Wilson introduced her to Motown founder Berry Gordy in the late 1950s. COMMODORES CO-FOUNDER AND FORMER BASSIST RONALD LAPREAD DEAD AT 75 She started working for Motown as a receptionist in 1958, but her role soon went well beyond answering phones. Like many employees in Motown’s early days, Bradford Hobbs became involved in making the music. She and Gordy wrote "Money (That’s What I Want)," which Barrett Strong recorded in 1959. The song became one of Motown’s first hits and was later recorded by The Beatles. Bradford Hobbs also wrote "Too Busy Thinking About My Baby." The Temptations recorded the song first, and Marvin Gaye later had a hit with it. She also wrote songs for Stevie Wonder, The Supremes, Martha & The Vandellas and others. "Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown, and she will always hold a very special place in my heart and in the Motown family," Gordy said in a statement. COUNTRY MUSIC ICON DON SCHLITZ, WHO WROTE KENNY ROGERS' HIT 'THE GAMBLER,' DEAD AT 73 Gordy described Bradford Hobbs as one of the people who believed in Motown before anyone knew what it would become. "Janie was one of a special group I have always thought of as the original Motown family — the unsung heroes who believed in the dream before anyone knew what Motown would become," Gordy continued. "She was one of the people who helped make Motown what it became." Bradford Hobbs later became head of Writer Relations for Jobete, Motown’s publishing company. After leaving Motown, she founded the annual Heroes and Legends Awards, which honored figures in the music industry and awarded scholarships for about 30 years, according to her family. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP She is survived by her husband, Wardean Hobbs; daughter, Nicole Hobbs; son, Lance Finney; and two grandsons. Funeral arrangements have not been completed. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: John Candy's family calls out Hollywood for weight criticism the actor endured throughout his career
articles.summary: Jennifer Candy-Sullivan and Rosemary Candy slam Hollywood's weight criticism of John Candy, revealing how the late comedian handled it privately.
articles.body: John Candy's family is calling out Hollywood for how their father was treated. During a recent interview with Fox News Digital at Televerse 26, the late actor's daughter, Jennifer Candy-Sullivan, and her mother Rosemary Candy, slammed Hollywood for the way their father's weight was discussed during his fame. "I think everyone who had some sort of difference was kind of put under a magnifying glass. So for him, it was his weight. And he kind of... he took it like a gentleman," Jennifer said. "And I think as his career went on, he was able to be more comfortable with himself and kind of vocalize and speak up for himself." She went on to say that because of his career, people "thought he was the everyday guy and everyone loved him" so it would be okay to "pal around" and "joke around him," but that "in reality, it wasn't that okay. It's not cool." JACK OSBOURNE FIRES BACK AT BODY SHAMERS CALLING HIM 'GROSSLY UNDERWEIGHT' Rosemary noted that "he was able to handle it really well," but that it was still "upsetting" and "a challenge" he was dealing with early in his career, "from the beginning when I met him." WATCH: John Candy’s daughter says actor ‘took it like a gentleman’ when Hollywood focused on his weight Jennifer doesn't think the public or the media would be any less harsh on her father if his rise to fame occurred today, saying, "I think there would be a different type of kind of critique to him." "I think if he tried losing weight, then it would be like, 'You're too skinny, you're no longer funny.' So I think Hollywood would find something," she said. "It would be... he doesn't... he would do something wrong. Ultimately, I think anyone in Hollywood does something wrong." The two attended a special FYC presentation of the documentary about the comedian, "John Candy: I Like Me," as part of Televerse 26, the Television Academy festival. The film, which originally premiered at the Toronto Film Festival in September 2025, was directed by Colin Hanks, and features interviews from many of his former co-stars, including Steve Martin, Macaulay Culkin, Bill Murray, Catherine O'Hara, Martin Short and others. WATCH: John Candy’s daughter says Hollywood would have criticized him even if he lost weight: ‘You’re too skinny’ "When we would see John on the screen, we felt like he was one of the most relatable people," Hanks said. "And I think in working on the film and talking with people and learning more about John's past, I just felt like we didn't even understand just how relatable he was." GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE He explained that talking "about things like mental health and therapy" has only become popular in recent years and "wasn't something that was discussed back then." With today's lenses on, "John was even more like one of us than we even realize." WATCH: John Candy's daughter got to see a vulnerable side of her father in the documentary 'John Candy: I Like Me' Hanks isn't the only one who learned something new about the "Planes, Trains and Automobiles" actor. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "I think for us, it was to see his vulnerability with those interviews. He was really good about keeping his business at work, and then family life was family life. So he tried not to bring it into the house," Jennifer said. "My mom probably understood it more because they would have conversations about it, obviously. But for us, we didn't really see it. So I think to see that on camera on the big screen was challenging." John rose to fame as a member of the sketch comedy show, "Second City Television," on which he also worked as a writer. His writing on the show earned him two Emmy Awards. WATCH: Colin Hanks calls John Candy 'one of the most relatable people' He later made his breakthrough in Hollywood in the movie, "Splash," and went on to star in a number of iconic films such as "Uncle Buck," "The Great Outdoors," "Spaceballs," "Cool Runnings" and many others. articles.title: Stella Lefty has an inescapable hit song and a billionaire dad. Music's nepo baby boom is getting harder to ignore
articles.summary: Stella Lefty says she understands the chatter about her father's wealth. As more nepo babies climb the charts, that conversation is only getting louder.
articles.body:
Maybe you've heard it on the radio recently or come by it by way of your Spotify algorithm: A raspy pop-country song about taking a train back to Boston and a budding relationship, from an emerging artist who seemed to come out of nowhere earlier this year. Her name is Stella Lefty.

Her monthly listeners on Spotify nearly doubled to 15 million in May, when her breakout song "Boston" made the cover of the platform's Hot Country playlist. In addition to the single climbing the Hot 100, the 24-year-old Chicago native just nabbed two VMA nominations and released a new album, Long Way Home , on Aug. 21 — altogether a massive summer for someone who wasn't signed by a major label until earlier this year.

But there's a fact about Lefty that I can't stop thinking about every time I hear her song, which is often: She's the daughter of a billionaire.

Lefty's dad is Eric Lefkofsky, the founder of Groupon and Tempus AI. He's worth an estimated $4.8 billion, per Forbes , which makes him one of the 1,000 richest people in the world. Does that make her rise — and the rise of the many other nepo babies breaking out in music right now — any less exciting?

A scroll through the charts at the moment will yield you a list of artists with successful parents, varying from those who simply have some industry connections to those who are undeniable household names. There's Audrey Hobert, the star of NPR's latest Tiny Desk whose dad is a writer and producer known for Scrubs and The Middle ; Malcolm Todd, Hobert's brother who just scored a Gap ad and a VMA nod; Gracie Abrams, daughter of blockbuster writer-director JJ Abrams; and VMA nominee Magnus Ferrell , son of comedian Will Ferrell. Being related to someone well-connected in the industry is hot right now.

"If a family connection gets you a meeting, I can't call that a scandal. It's natural for a parent to open any door they can for their child. Most of us would do the same," Jay Siegan, a longtime music executive, tells Yahoo.

It's the most surefire way to skip past the pesky "unknown" phase of stardom and get access to resources that artists with day jobs don't have. But Siegan notes that "the door only stays open once. The audience is the great equalizer, and either someone resonates, or they don't."

The boom in stars with famous lineage isn't entirely new. What's different now, compared to the past when nepo artists like Ziggy Marley, Hank Williams Jr. and Rosanne Cash were developing their own careers with a boost from their parents' coattails, is just how much we're talking about it. Nepotism has become an obsession in the 2020s, in a world where people are constantly suspicious that there are unseen influences everywhere. It's hard not to resent the people who seem to have been born with a leg up in life .

Multiple music industry publicists tell Yahoo that it's best to be upfront about nepotism status from the beginning, because it'll inevitably become something the public fixates on. Maxwell James, who works in entertainment publicity, says he'd recommend "acknowledging the advantage without making it the center of the artist's identity."

No matter how hard you try to downplay it, audiences can tell when artists have benefitted from access, resources, relationships and early exposure, James explains. They'll need to prove themselves with their talent, showing that they belong at the upper echelon just as much as someone who's gifted but didn't get a head start.

In a recent interview with Vanity Fair, Lefty says it's obvious to her that there's going to be chatter about her father's wealth, "which I totally understand." "Me and my dad have spoken about this a lot since I even started music. He was like, 'The truth will set you free,'" she says. The interview didn't reveal any more of her thoughts on how her parentage affected her career, though.

There's really no denying that nepo babies have opportunities that other artists don't. For instance, Magnus Ferrell got an instant boost in fame when his dad played a snippet of his song on Michelle Obama's podcast this summer, though he wasn't necessarily an overnight success. Many of them also had parents rich enough that they never had to approach "starving artist" territory. Not needing a day job while you plug away at your craft is a massive luxury.

James says the worst thing a nepo baby can do is appear defensive about whether they "deserve" their success. Gracie Abrams was praised for acknowledging in an interview with the New York Times' Popcast that she has "privilege" and a "safety net" afforded to her by her parents' status in Hollywood — and their wealth. "That allowed me the ability to experiment and to concentrate and I had the gift of time to dedicate to doing this thing I loved. I wasn't growing up afraid financially, and that's the biggest deal," she says.

That may elide, nevertheless, what really matters: connections. Those contacts could be vaguely in entertainment, where a meeting can go a long way, or it could be specifically within the opaque music industry. There's a difference between Billie Eilish's parents , who were working actors, and Clairo's dad, who was a high-level marketing exec with label connections. That sparked debate about which artists might be industry plants , a common concern among music fans worried that an up-and-coming star might be "planted" on the charts by record labels, rendering them inauthentic and unworthy of their success.

Nepotism doesn't guarantee success, of course. Plenty of celebrity and industry children try and fail, while random singers take off on TikTok all the time. Though let's be honest — any breakout success on an algorithm-driven platform, be it a streaming service or a social media site, can always have paid promotion behind it. As I type this, there's a massive ad for Lefty's album dominating my Spotify homepage.

Nickie Robinson, a music marketer, notes that a lot of these nepo babies honed their talent in the first place because they could afford tutoring and lessons from a young age. She sees it as a gift, but one that should be acknowledged by the beneficiary.

"Remember, labels only care about numbers, and most nepo babies have a substantial following from their parents and associated proximity bias. Why not leverage it?" she says, admitting they sometimes get on her nerves when she notices how plainly their parents can open doors for them. But, just like everyone else, they have the option to ignore the haters and just keep working.

"In this industry, you cannot care what people think. They will always have something to say, regardless," she says. Might as well let them.

There's Audrey Hobert, the star of NPR's latest Tiny Desk whose dad is a writer and producer known for Scrubs and The Middle ; Malcolm Todd, Hobert's brother who just scored a Gap ad and a VMA nod; Gracie Abrams, daughter of blockbuster writer-director JJ Abrams; and VMA nominee Magnus Ferrell , son of comedian Will Ferrell. Being related to someone well-connected in the industry is hot right now.

"If a family connection gets you a meeting, I can't call that a scandal. It's natural for a parent to open any door they can for their child. Most of us would do the same," Jay Siegan, a longtime music executive, tells Yahoo.

It's the most surefire way to skip past the pesky "unknown" phase of stardom and get access to resources that artists with day jobs don't have. But Siegan notes that "the door only stays open once. The audience is the great equalizer, and either someone resonates, or they don't."

The boom in stars with famous lineage isn't entirely new. What's different now, compared to the past when nepo artists like Ziggy Marley, Hank Williams Jr. and Rosanne Cash were developing their own careers with a boost from their parents' coattails, is just how much we're talking about it. Nepotism has become an obsession in the 2020s, in a world where people are constantly suspicious that there are unseen influences everywhere. It's hard not to resent the people who seem to have been born with a leg up in life .

Multiple music industry publicists tell Yahoo that it's best to be upfront about nepotism status from the beginning, because it'll inevitably become something the public fixates on. Maxwell James, who works in entertainment publicity, says he'd recommend "acknowledging the advantage without making it the center of the artist's identity."

No matter how hard you try to downplay it, audiences can tell when artists have benefitted from access, resources, relationships and early exposure, James explains. They'll need to prove themselves with their talent, showing that they belong at the upper echelon just as much as someone who's gifted but didn't get a head start.

In a recent interview with Vanity Fair, Lefty says it's obvious to her that there's going to be chatter about her father's wealth, "which I totally understand." "Me and my dad have spoken about this a lot since I even started music. He was like, 'The truth will set you free,'" she says. The interview didn't reveal any more of her thoughts on how her parentage affected her career, though.

There's really no denying that nepo babies have opportunities that other artists don't. For instance, Magnus Ferrell got an instant boost in fame when his dad played a snippet of his song on Michelle Obama's podcast this summer, though he wasn't necessarily an overnight success. Many of them also had parents rich enough that they never had to approach "starving artist" territory. Not needing a day job while you plug away at your craft is a massive luxury.

James says the worst thing a nepo baby can do is appear defensive about whether they "deserve" their success. Gracie Abrams was praised for acknowledging in an interview with the New York Times' Popcast that she has "privilege" and a "safety net" afforded to her by her parents' status in Hollywood — and their wealth. "That allowed me the ability to experiment and to concentrate and I had the gift of time to dedicate to doing this thing I loved. I wasn't growing up afraid financially, and that's the biggest deal," she says.

That may elide, nevertheless, what really matters: connections. Those contacts could be vaguely in entertainment, where a meeting can go a long way, or it could be specifically within the opaque music industry. There's a difference between Billie Eilish's parents , who were working actors, and Clairo's dad, who was a high-level marketing exec with label connections. That sparked debate about which artists might be industry plants , a common concern among music fans worried that an up-and-coming star might be "planted" on the charts by record labels, rendering them inauthentic and unworthy of their success.

Nepotism doesn't guarantee success, of course. Plenty of celebrity and industry children try and fail, while random singers take off on TikTok all the time. Though let's be honest — any breakout success on an algorithm-driven platform, be it a streaming service or a social media site, can always have paid promotion behind it. As I type this, there's a massive ad for Lefty's album dominating my Spotify homepage.

Nickie Robinson, a music marketer, notes that a lot of these nepo babies honed their talent in the first place because they could afford tutoring and lessons from a young age. She sees it as a gift, but one that should be acknowledged by the beneficiary.

"Remember, labels only care about numbers, and most nepo babies have a substantial following from their parents and associated proximity bias. Why not leverage it?" she says, admitting they sometimes get on her nerves when she notices how plainly their parents can open doors for them. But, just like everyone else, they have the option to ignore the haters and just keep working.
"In this industry, you cannot care what people think. They will always have something to say, regardless," she says. Might as well let them.

articles.title: Hayden Panettiere’s mom discloses heartbreaking ultimatum in their final phone call before actress’ death
articles.summary: Hayden Panettiere's mom reveals the therapist-advised ultimatum over Brian Hickerson that led to their estrangement months before the actress' death.
articles.body: Hayden Panettiere's mom is detailing the heartbreaking ultimatum that led to their estrangement months before the actress' death. In an interview with "Good Morning America," which aired Monday, Lesley Vogel said she and the late actress had become estranged in the months before Panettiere's death after Vogel gave her daughter an ultimatum over her daughter's relationship with on-again, off-again boyfriend Brian Hickerson. About a year ago, Vogel traveled to California to stay with Panettiere and help her end her relationship with Hickerson — a decision the "Nashville" star made on her own, Vogel claimed. HAYDEN PANETTIERE'S MOTHER POINTS FINGER AT BRIAN HICKERSON AFTER 'NASHVILLE' STAR'S DEATH AT 36 "She knew that Brian was toxic," Vogel said. "She knew she had to get him out of her life." Vogel said things began to change after about six weeks, when she noticed her daughter slowly pulling away. It was then that she returned home to Florida. HAYDEN PANETTIERE AND THE CHILD STARS WHOSE RELATIONSHIPS WITH THEIR MOMAGERS TURNED COMPLICATED "When I got the phone call from her saying, ‘I’m going to be with the person I love,’ … I just lost it," Vogel recalled. "I could not believe that she had gone that far back, that he had been successful in reeling her back in with all of the things he had done to her." Vogel said that, on the advice of her therapist, she told Panettiere that she could no longer speak with her as long as Hickerson remained part of her life. The decision marked the beginning of their estrangement — something Vogel believed would only be temporary. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "I needed to have that pocket of time," she said. "Of course, I thought it was going to be a pocket of time. I did not by any stretch of the imagination think that this was going to happen to Hayden." "I don’t know why, I just didn’t," she added. "Maybe I didn’t want to." Panettiere was found dead inside a Greenville, South Carolina residence on Aug. 16. POLICE SHOW UP AT HOME LINKED TO HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S ON-AND-OFF BOYFRIEND DAYS AFTER HER SUDDEN DEATH Hickerson and his brother, Zach, called 911 after finding the actress unresponsive, according to a police report obtained by Fox News Digital. Hickerson later gave authorities a bag containing medication Panettiere had been taking, according to the report. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE Preliminary autopsy results found no signs of trauma that contributed to Panettiere’s death, the Greenville County Coroner's Office confirmed to Fox News Digital. However, Panettiere's death remains under investigation. HAYDEN PANETTIERE REMEMBERED BY VIOLA DAVIS, BETHANY JOY LENZ AND OTHER CELEBRITIES AFTER SUDDEN DEATH AT 36 Fox News has learned the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) has also been contacted and is assisting with the investigation. Vogel told "GMA" that Panettiere lived a very "happy life" until her late teens. DISNEY ALUM CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RIPS HOLLYWOOD FOR FAILING CHILD STARS AFTER HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S DEATH "I would say at about 17, I started seeing her going downhill," Vogel said. "As she got older, and it wasn’t my voice anymore. I wasn’t in charge of her choices." Panettiere's decision to give up custody of her daughter, Kaya — whom she shared with former fiancé Wladimir Klitschko — was a turning point, Vogel said. HAYDEN PANETTIERE DEFENDS GIVING UP CUSTODY OF HER DAUGHTER DESPITE INTENSE 'EMOTIONAL PAIN' "Vlad had taken over custody, you know, for safety," Vogel said. "In my opinion, that was the catalyst that she just couldn’t keep those demons away." In an interview with the New York Times, Vogel said her daughter was living with chronic physical pain. "She was in pain," Vogel said. "She was afraid. She couldn’t physically function properly." Vogel said she brought Panettiere to multiple doctors and pursued massage and acupuncture treatments to address the "pins and needles" sensation the actress often experienced in her lower extremities. PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE Ultimately, Vogel said, she hopes her daughter will be remembered for the "talented, beautiful, outgoing, intelligent woman" she was. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "She really was," Vogel told "GMA". "But I also want people to understand that it is my belief that she was suffering. Now that doesn't make sense because when you look at a beautiful girl who's got an incredible career, even though it has had its ups and downs, but, you look at that big picture, and you go, 'Why would you be suffering?' People don't understand that you can have, on the exterior, all of this, but that doesn't mean that what's going on in here matches." Fox News Digital's Lauryn Overhultz contributed to this report.

articles.title: Meghan Markle's rumored return to acting in Netflix's 'The Gentlemen' draws conflicting reports
articles.summary: Reports link the Duchess of Sussex to Guy Ritchie's "The Gentlemen." She hasn't taken a scripted role since leaving "Suits" in 2018.
articles.body:
Meghan Markle's reported return to acting continues to generate speculation, with conflicting accounts as to whether the Duchess of Sussex is being lined up to star in Guy Ritchie's Netflix crime drama The Gentlemen following her U.K. move .

Deadline first reported on the rumors that Meghan could join the show's cast last week but cautioned that talks were hypothetical, in part because Netflix had yet to officially renew The Gentlemen beyond its second season, which premieres Sept. 3.

On Monday, while releasing the trailer for the show's second season, the streaming giant confirmed that Season 3 is coming, with Ritchie back to direct. In a statement, Ritchie wrote: "A third season felt inevitable, and I'm looking forward to pushing the boundaries of it further."

No mention of Meghan was made, however, leaving a lingering question mark hanging over any potential role she may play in the show.

On Saturday, Tina Brown, the former editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair and The New Yorker, reported that the offer had been withdrawn, citing a backlash in the U.K. Brown, a prominent journalist who is widely regarded as an expert on the royals, wrote in a Substack column: "I learned this morning that the casting of Meghan Markle in season 3 of Guy Ritchie's Netflix series The Gentlemen has been withdrawn. The backlash in the UK was so intense, it became untenable to go forward. This does not bode well for Meghan's acting comeback in the UK."

However, U.K. newspaper The Sun reported on Sunday that Meghan remained in talks to star in the show, citing an unnamed source as stating "no formal agreement has been reached." An additional account reported by The Times of London on Sunday suggested that Netflix executives had been unaware of any preliminary offer.

Sources close to the Sussexes have not denied that Meghan was offered a role, the BBC reported. Bronte Coy, the news.com.au reporter who first reported it, told BBC Radio 4 the project is a "top secret" U.K. production and that it played a "significant" part in the family's decision to return.

Meghan, her husband Prince Harry and their two young children are reportedly moving back to the U.K. this month , ahead of their children starting school in Britain in September. The Associated Press reported that they have already been enrolled, citing a person close to the Sussexes who was not authorized to speak publicly.

According to ABC News , the couple hasn't decided how long they will stay in the U.K. They plan to remain for an "extended period of time," according to a source familiar with the matter.

Apart from a recent cameo as herself in the Amazon MGM Studios movie Close Personal Friends , which stars Lily Collins and Brie Larson and is currently in post-production, Meghan's acting career has been on hold since her last episode of Suits aired in 2018. She played paralegal Rachel Zane in the USA Network legal drama for seven seasons.

Much of Meghan's recent television work has centered on the Netflix lifestyle series With Love, Meghan , which she hosted and executive-produced. The 2025 series grew out of Meghan and Harry's wider relationship with Netflix. In September 2020, eight months after stepping back from their duties as senior royals, the couple signed a deal with the streaming service through what would become their production company, Archewell Productions. The deal was widely reported to be worth around $100 million.

Their Netflix projects have included the six-part 2022 documentary series Harry & Meghan , Live to Lead (2022), a docuseries profiling prominent activists and leaders; Heart of Invictus (2023), which followed competitors preparing for the Invictus Games; and Polo (2024), a five-part series about players competing in the U.S. Open Polo Championship.

In August 2025, Netflix announced that Archewell Productions had signed a new multiyear first-look deal covering its film and television projects. The terms were not disclosed. Their new output included the second season of With Love, Meghan and a holiday special in December 2025.

Alongside her potential return to acting, the BBC reported that Meghan hopes to expand the global reach of her U.S.-based lifestyle and cooking brand, As Ever, after returning to the U.K. A partnership between the brand and Netflix helped launch it, but the streaming giant stepped down as a backer in March. "As it was always intended, Meghan will continue growing the brand and take it into its next chapter independently," a Netflix spokesperson told Variety at the time.

Upon their reported return to the U.K., the Sussexes are expected to settle in a privately owned home outside London rather than a royal property, according to the Associated Press. They also intend to keep their Montecito, Calif., home and a vacation property in Portugal. Harry and Meghan do not plan to resume their roles as working members of the royal family.

The Daily Telegraph was the first outlet to report the plans. People magazine subsequently reported on the relocation, while Reuters said a source close to Harry and Meghan had confirmed the plans.

Neither a spokesperson for Harry and Meghan nor Buckingham Palace has publicly confirmed the move. Harry said he had "nothing to say" when asked about the reports Wednesday night during an event with U.S. veterans in Washington.

The reported move comes as Harry has sought to repair his relationship with his family, particularly his father, King Charles III.

articles.title: Melissa Gilbert pleads to protect child actors after Hayden Panettiere's death at 36
articles.summary: Melissa Gilbert named three female child actors who died within one year as she demanded real substantive change for young performers.
articles.body: Melissa Gilbert made a passionate plea for child actors in the wake of Hayden Panettiere's death. Gilbert, 62, admitted that she didn't personally know the "Heroes" actress, but took Panettiere's death personally as she begged for industry changes in a post shared on Substack. "Within one year, Michelle Trachtenberg, Daveigh Chase and Hayden Panettiere have died," Gilbert wrote. "Three former female child actors of the same generation are gone. Tragically, heartbreakingly, agonizingly too soon." HAYDEN PANETTIERE'S CO-STAR JUSTIN CHATWIN 'P----- OFF' OVER HOLLYWOOD CULTURE AFTER HER PASSING "They are gone and the question I have been turning over and over in my head is, ‘WHY?". Why are these three sweet, wildly talented, vibrant, vital young women gone?" Trachtenberg died naturally of complications from diabetes mellitus in February 2025. She was 39. HAYDEN PANETTIERE'S FINAL PETA CAMPAIGN CAPTURED WEEKS BEFORE HER DEATH MARKED LIFETIME OF ADVOCACY WORK Chase died in June from acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), according to the Los Angeles Medical Examiner's office. She was 35. "And why does this all feel so personal to me? I did not know Hayden personally and only worked briefly with Mishy and Daveigh," she wrote. "It feels personal because I was them. As were Tatum, Kristy, Brooke, Patty, Anyssa, Dakota, Elle, Shirley, Britney, Jodie, Drew and my sister Sara, to name a few." Gilbert wrote that the women were "all members of the same tribe" she coined the "Female Former Child Performers," and wrote that one member dies, "it runs through all of us like an electrical current." "When three of us die so close together, something is very, very wrong," Gilbert wrote before arguing that while "a combination of many factors," could be to blame – including the invention of cell phones heightening mental health issues – the collective society should "lobby for and enact, real substantive change." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "All I know is something has got to be done," she wrote. "I have this image in my mind of Hayden’s little girl who will now grow up without her Mama. She is eleven years old. That’s the same age I was when my father died." Gilbert added, "And now I am weeping as I type this and I just want to scream from the rooftops, "ENOUGH!'" WLADIMIR KLITSCHKO MOURNS FORMER FIANCÉE HAYDEN PANETTIERE, VOWS TO KEEP HER MEMORY ALIVE FOR DAUGHTER KAYA The "Nashville" actress died Aug 16 in Greenville, South Carolina. Brian Hickerson and his brother, Zach Hickerson, were with Panettiere at the time of her death, according to a police report. Preliminary autopsy results found no signs of trauma that contributed to her death, Fox News Digital confirmed. The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) was contacted and is assisting in the investigation. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE The "Little House on the Prairie" star's plea came as her husband, Timothy Busfield, awaits trial on multiple counts of criminal sexual contact with a child after two boys accused him of child sexual abuse on set of the production "The Cleaning Lady." Busfield entered a not guilty plea in February, according to New Mexico court records reviewed by Fox News Digital. He also waived his right to an arraignment and other pretrial proceedings. The "Thirtysomething" star, 68, surrendered to local authorities on child sex abuse charges Jan. 13. He was held without bail at the time of his arrest on two counts of criminal sexual contact of a minor and one count of child abuse.  Busfield's attorney, Larry Stein, insisted the case against his client "cannot be proven at trial" in a statement shared with Fox News Digital following his indictment. PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE "The indictment was not unexpected. As the saying goes, a grand jury will indict a ham sandwich," Stein said. articles.title: Former child star Raquel Lee Bolleau alleges sexual assault on Disney Channel movie set
articles.summary: In a lawsuit filed last week, Bolleau claims Disney ignored signs she was being sexually abused while on set of the 2001 film “The Poof Point.”
articles.body: Former child actor Raquel Lee Bolleau alleges in a lawsuit filed last week that a male Disney employee sexually assaulted her while she was filming a network movie in 2001 and that the studio failed to respond to signs of abuse. Bolleau was 14 at the time of the alleged attacks, which she said unfolded during the filming of the Disney Channel movie “The Poof Point.” The plaintiff, now 39, said her alleged attacker, who is not named in the suit, was “a lifelong resident of California” who was more than twice as old as she was at the time. “John Doe” was “an on-set, adult, middle-aged, male employee of Disney who was involved in the filming of the movie” who “repeatedly raped, sexually assaulted, sexually abused and sexually harassed” Bolleau, according to the suit, which was filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court on Friday. “Mr. Doe’s sexual abuse of Ms. Bolleau was apparent to the adults on Disney’s set,” the suit states. “Disney repeatedly failed Ms. Bolleau.” A representative of Disney, based in Burbank, California, could not be immediately reached for comment Monday. Bolleau’s other credits include voicing Olei on Disney’s “The Proud Family: Louder and Prouder,” and Nubia Gross in “The Proud Family” original series and movie, according to IMDb. She has also appeared in shows like “Real Husbands of Hollywood” and films like “Stan the Man.” She alleges the abuse she experienced derailed her career because she had “trauma of returning to a set,” according to the lawsuit. Her lawsuit comes amid growing scrutiny of how child performers have been treated in Hollywood. The 2024 documentary “Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV” detailed allegations of toxic working conditions on some Nickelodeon shows. Bolleau participated in the documentary, where she opened up about her experiences as a Black actor on “The Amanda Show,” but she did not discuss the allegations made in her recent lawsuit. Other former child stars have since spoken about the pressures of growing up in the industry and called for stronger support. Protections for child performers have expanded over the past decade, including new on-set advocates and tighter rules for adults working with minors. But industry sources told NBC News last week that safeguards remain inconsistent and have not kept pace with growing awareness of the potential mental health effects of child stardom. The alleged abuse toward Bolleau occurred in Utah, where “The Poof Point” was filmed, often in the man’s hotel room after he supplied her with alcohol, as well as on set, according to the lawsuit. “On set, Mr. Doe regularly fondled and excessively touched Ms. Bolleau, often rubbing his genitals on Ms. Bolleau while giving her unsolicited hugs,” the suit states. “No one from Disney stopped this extremely inappropriate touching and molestation of a child.” The abuse continued after the cast left Salt Lake City, with the man sexually assaulting Bolleau under a blanket as they flew back to California, the lawsuit said. Bolleau’s work on “The Poof Point” suffered due to the alcohol and sex, according to the lawsuit. “Disney recognized Ms. Bolleau’s sudden shift in demeanor and performance — clear indicia of child sexual abuse — and attacked, blamed and threatened Ms. Bolleau, a victim of rape, and Ms. Bolleau’s mother,” according to the lawsuit. The studio “has been protecting and empowering sexual predators,” the lawsuit adds. It’s unclear whether Bolleau or her guardian reported the 2001 assaults to the police. The suit does not mention any police involvement. Bolleau’s legal team declined to comment on whether law enforcement had ever been notified. Salt Lake City Police Detective Michael Ruff told NBC News in a statement Monday, “We do not have any records involving the name provided.” “There over a dozen police departments in Salt Lake County, without further details it’s difficult to know if the accusations occurred within our jurisdiction,” Ruff said. Bolleau’s lawsuit does not specify the amount of damages she is seeking. “Over the last decade, countless child actors have come forward to bravely share their experiences of abuse by adults in entertainment,” Bolleau’s attorneys, Douglas Wigdor and Jane Kim, said in a statement, adding that those responsible “directly or indirectly” should be held accountable.

articles.title: Kashmera Shah backs Sunita Ahuja after she withdrew divorce petition and claimed Govinda planned to marry Komal Rani Swarnkar: âI will stand with the women in my familyâ
articles.summary: The ongoing turmoil surrounding Govinda and Sunita Ahujaâs marriage has once again put their family in the spotlight. Amid reports of a possible divor.
articles.body: The ongoing turmoil surrounding Govinda and Sunita Ahujaâs marriage has once again put their family in the spotlight. Amid reports of a possible divorce, Sunitaâs public remarks about her relationship with Govinda and rumours linking the actor to actress Komal Rani Swarnkar, Kashmera Shah was asked to react to the situation.Kashmera, who is married to Govindaâs nephew Krushna Abhishek, refused to discuss every detail of the family matter but made one thing clear that she stands with the women in her family.Kashmera Shah says, âI will protect my familyâSpeaking to the paparazzi at Abhishek Kumarâs birthday celebration, Kashmera was asked about the ongoing controversy.She said, âMain itna jaanti hoon ki woh meri family hai, main apni family ko protect karungi, aur main apni family ki auraton ke saath khadi hoon.âKashmera then appeared to extend her support to Sunita, saying, âMain Sunita ke saath hoon.âShe also suggested that Sunitaâs decision to speak publicly should not be dismissed.âUnhone aaj tak kabhi awaaz uthayi hai, kabhi kaha hai ki ye galat hai, wo galat hai? Aaj bol rahi hai na, toh hoga kuchh galat hai. Dekh lo,â Kashmera said.Divorce buzz surrounding Govinda and Sunita AhujaKashmeraâs comments come amid renewed speculation about Govinda and Sunitaâs marriage. Reports about their alleged marital troubles and divorce have been circulating for months, with Sunita also making several public comments about their relationship.The situation gained further attention after Sunita was heard telling Rakhi Sawant on a phone call that she had withdrawn her divorce petition after learning that Govinda allegedly planned to marry actress Komal Rani Swarnkar.However, the claims surrounding Govinda and Komal Rani Swarnkar remain part of the ongoing public controversy, and Govinda has pushed back against reports and allegations concerning his personal life.Sunita Ahujaâs remarks about GovindaSunita has spoken openly about the difficulties in her marriage and has made allegations regarding Govindaâs alleged relationships.In one recent interaction with paparazzi, she reportedly referred to Govinda as a âsugar daddyâ to a new heroine, indirectly referring to Komal, and alleged that he was having an affair.The remarks fuelled further speculation about the coupleâs marriage and sparked widespread discussion online.Govinda later responded through a video message, asking people to stop abusing him and suggesting that his being paired opposite a younger actress did not mean he was romantically involved with her.Kashmera and Sunitaâs past feudKashmeraâs decision to support Sunita is particularly significant because the two women had a long-standing feud.Kashmera and Sunita were once openly estranged and reportedly did not speak to each other for years. Their relationship eventually improved, and the two reconciled after their nearly decade-long family dispute.Since then, Kashmera has spoken more warmly about Sunita and their relationship.Govinda issues legal warning amid rumoursAmid the controversy, Govinda has also taken legal steps to protect his reputation.The actor recently issued a public notice warning media outlets, digital platforms and social media users against publishing or sharing false, defamatory or unverified claims about him or his family.The notice reportedly includes warnings against AI-generated content, deepfakes, morphed photographs and manipulated videos involving Govinda and his family.It also states that civil and criminal action could be pursued against those responsible for defamatory or misleading content, with claims of up to Rs 100 crore reportedly being threatened.Kashmera had earlier questioned whether true love existsKashmeraâs latest comments also come shortly after she shared a cryptic social media post about marriage and infidelity.Sharing an image of a heart-shaped trail in the sky, she questioned whether âtrue loveâ still exists and admitted to feeling disillusioned by marriages ending and people cheating.Her post came amid the growing public discussion around Govinda and Sunitaâs marriage, prompting speculation among social media users about whether she was referring to the situation within her extended family.Give your child the gift of confidence! articles.title: Simon Cowell to miss weeks of ‘AGT’ filming as old injuries send him to surgery
articles.summary: Simon Cowell will miss weeks of "America's Got Talent" filming for a medical procedure tied to back issues from his 2020 electric bike accident.
articles.body: Simon Cowell is stepping away from the judges’ table. The longtime "America’s Got Talent" judge will miss weeks of filming as he prepares to undergo a medical procedure related to lingering back issues, Fox News Digital has learned. The show is in the process of scheduling guest judges to fill in during Cowell's absence. TMZ reported the procedure is routine and tied to Cowell’s longstanding back problems, rather than a new or serious health concern. 'AMERICA'S GOT TALENT' JUDGES CLASH OVER COUNTRY SINGER'S BOLD ORIGINAL PERFORMANCE Cowell has struggled with back issues since his electric-bike accident in 2020. "It could have been a lot worse. When I saw the X-ray, I really nearly smashed my spine to pieces, so I literally wouldn’t (have) been able to walk," he told Extra six months after his accident. The TV personality admitted he immediately knew he had broken his back after falling off the bike. I mean, it was just surreal," he told the outlet. Cowell was later injured in another e-bike incident in 2022. At the time, a source told Fox News Digital that Cowell had "crashed to the ground" and "broke his arm." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? articles.title: Kacey Musgraves divides fans with immigrant children’s plea, faces boycott calls to ‘shut up and sing’
articles.summary: Kacey Musgraves asked fans to donate to the Young Center for Immigrant Children's Rights during her tour opener, sparking a divided reaction on social media.
articles.body: Kacey Musgraves is facing backlash after asking fans to donate to an immigrant children’s rights group as her birthday wish while kicking off her "Middle of Nowhere" tour. On Friday, the country music star marked her 38th birthday on the opening night of her tour at the United Center in Chicago, Illinois. At one point, Musgraves paused her show and urged concertgoers to contribute to the Young Center for Immigrant Children's Rights. "It’s a wonderful organization, and they help give aid — legal aid — and money to children whose parents have been deported unfairly," Musgraves said. "It’s not a political thing. It’s just, these kids need help." She continued, "They have no guidance and no way to get through this thing without their homebase or their parents. So anyway, 50 cents, whatever the hell, I don't know, whatever you want to do but that would mean a lot to me." KACEY MUSGRAVES FACES BOYCOTT CALLS AFTER ASKING FANS TO DONATE TO IMMIGRANT CHILDREN'S GROUP "If you don't want to, that's totally fine too," Musgraves added. The eight-time Grammy Award winner's appeal was immediately met with applause and cheers from the crowd in Chicago. However, Musgraves' request drew a divided response online, including criticism from conservative political commentators. "What is an unfair deportation?" Tomi Lahren, host of Outkick's "Tomi Lahren Is Fearless" podcast, wrote on X alongside a video of Musgraves' birthday request. KENNY CHESNEY TELLS BILL MAHER THE KEY REASON HE REFUSES TO TELL HIS LISTENERS HOW TO VOTE "Kacey Musgraves stopped her concert to ask the audience to donate money for legal aid to kids whose parents have been deported ‘unfairly.’ How about donating money the help kids who's parents have been killed by illegal immigrants! What happened to the country music industry?" conservative influencer Vince Langman commented. "Another TRAITOROUS woman who wants nothing more than to see our country fall," an X user chimed in. "Shut up and sing Kasey (sic)!! Why do musicians think they Can draw a line in the sand? You alienate 50% of your audience," another commented. Some critics declared that they would no longer support Musgraves and called for a boycott of her music and concerts. NATALIE MAINES’ ANTI-TRUMP TIRADE, ZACH BRYAN’S FENCE-CLIMBING CLASH FUEL COUNTRY MUSIC’S BIGGEST FEUDS "You just earned yourself a big ol’ boycott, you traitor," one detractor wrote. "Illegal aliens and their kids don’t deserve our patronage and neither do you!" "I’m deporting Musgraves from all my music playlists," another X user commented. Other social media users argued that Musgraves should donate her own money rather than ask fans to contribute. "Kacey Musgraves is worth $15 million. Yet she’s asking fans who already paid $150 to $350 for tickets to donate to support the children of illegal aliens," one social media user commented. "If she cares that much, she can fund it herself and let them live in one of her multi-million-dollar mansions." MUSICIAN KENNY CHESNEY'S REFUSAL TO SPEAK OUT ON POLITICS SPARKS ARGUMENT ON 'THE VIEW' "Everyone she is speaking too (sic) gave her their money when they bought tickets," another added. "She did not give the audience money. So now she has the money, shouldn't she donate to whatever cause she wants? She is actually on stage at a show that the audience had to pay to get admission to and now she is asking for more of their money. That's rude." However, some of the "Dry Spell" singer's fans defended her on social media and praised her for speaking out on behalf of immigrant children. POP STAR OLIVIA RODRIGO FELT 'ENRAGED' AFTER ICE USED HER HIT SONG, BRANDS AGENCY 'BARBARIC' "Love this. 'It's not a political thing. It's just, these kids need help.' Exactly. More artists doing this please," one fan wrote on X. "In all fairness, the kids didn’t do anything wrong," another wrote. "I don’t believe their parents were wrongfully deported, but I equally believe that their children, if retained in the United States by law, should be taken care of. We’re not f------ animals!" "No boycott here!" an X user declared. "Helping children caught in difficult circumstances is a worthy cause," one commenter argued. "At the same time, immigration enforcement and whether a deportation was lawful or justified are matters for the courts and policymakers not concert stages." Fox News Digital has reached out to Musgraves' representatives for comment. Meanwhile, Musgraves stood by her remarks on social media, taking to her Instagram Story to upload a post that read, "Kinda chic when kids don't face immigration court alone." The singer also reposted a message shared by the Young Center's Instagram page, in which the organization expressed its gratitude to her. "Thank you," the nonprofit wrote. "We appreciate your support of our work and mission to see unaccompanied immigrant children safe, free, and with their families." Based in Chicago, the Young Center describes its work as pairing volunteers with attorneys and social workers to advocate for unaccompanied and separated immigrant children in government custody. Its website lists family unity, release from custody, fair proceedings and children's best interests among its priorities. The nonprofit reported serving 1,975 children from 53 countries in 2024 and opening 1,388 new cases. Its 2025 annual report said children's average detention time increased from 30 to 198 days and requests for assistance from detained parents quadrupled from 2024. Friday’s appeal extended Musgraves’ support for the charity. In April, resale platform Depop announced that 20 pieces from her wardrobe, including clothing from music videos and tours, would be sold in capsule drops. Women's Wear Daily reported that all proceeds would benefit the Young Center. In announcing the sale, Musgraves described the beneficiary without discussing immigration enforcement. "I also adore the fact that the sales are supporting a really beautiful cause," Musgraves said. Musgraves also invited three brothers, ages 18, 14 and 12, to open three Texas shows in May after their family was released from ICE custody. The mariachi performers' family said they entered through the now-defunct CBP One appointment system in 2023 and sought asylum after fleeing violence in Mexico, KSAT reported. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE DHS said the family entered illegally and had been released into the country by the Biden administration. Responding to the family’s detention, DHS said federal law required custody while its immigration claims were heard. "The law requires illegal aliens who show up at a port of entry without valid entry to be detained while all their claims are heard. You can look it up in the statute," a DHS spokesperson told KSAT. "Unlike the previous administration, the Trump administration is not going to ignore the rule of law." Musgraves' latest remarks came as ICE enforcement reached record levels. Federal sources told Fox News Digital that agents made about 51,000 immigration arrests in July, topping the previous record of roughly 43,000 in June. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? Official tour listings showed dates continuing through October. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital's CJ Womack contributed to this report.

KENNY CHESNEY TELLS BILL MAHER THE KEY REASON HE REFUSES TO TELL HIS LISTENERS HOW TO VOTE "Kacey Musgraves stopped her concert to ask the audience to donate money for legal aid to kids whose parents have been deported ‘unfairly.’ How about donating money the help kids who's parents have been killed by illegal immigrants! What happened to the country music industry?" conservative influencer Vince Langman commented. "Another TRAITOROUS woman who wants nothing more than to see our country fall," an X user chimed in. "Shut up and sing Kasey (sic)!! Why do musicians think they Can draw a line in the sand? You alienate 50% of your audience," another commented. Some critics declared that they would no longer support Musgraves and called for a boycott of her music and concerts. NATALIE MAINES’ ANTI-TRUMP TIRADE, ZACH BRYAN’S FENCE-CLIMBING CLASH FUEL COUNTRY MUSIC’S BIGGEST FEUDS "You just earned yourself a big ol’ boycott, you traitor," one detractor wrote. "Illegal aliens and their kids don’t deserve our patronage and neither do you!" "I’m deporting Musgraves from all my music playlists," another X user commented. Other social media users argued that Musgraves should donate her own money rather than ask fans to contribute. "Kacey Musgraves is worth $15 million. Yet she’s asking fans who already paid $150 to $350 for tickets to donate to support the children of illegal aliens," one social media user commented. "If she cares that much, she can fund it herself and let them live in one of her multi-million-dollar mansions." MUSICIAN KENNY CHESNEY'S REFUSAL TO SPEAK OUT ON POLITICS SPARKS ARGUMENT ON 'THE VIEW' "Everyone she is speaking too (sic) gave her their money when they bought tickets," another added. "She did not give the audience money. So now she has the money, shouldn't she donate to whatever cause she wants? She is actually on stage at a show that the audience had to pay to get admission to and now she is asking for more of their money. That's rude." However, some of the "Dry Spell" singer's fans defended her on social media and praised her for speaking out on behalf of immigrant children. POP STAR OLIVIA RODRIGO FELT 'ENRAGED' AFTER ICE USED HER HIT SONG, BRANDS AGENCY 'BARBARIC' "Love this. 'It's not a political thing. It's just, these kids need help.' Exactly. More artists doing this please," one fan wrote on X. "In all fairness, the kids didn’t do anything wrong," another wrote. "I don’t believe their parents were wrongfully deported, but I equally believe that their children, if retained in the United States by law, should be taken care of. We’re not f------ animals!" "No boycott here!" an X user declared. "Helping children caught in difficult circumstances is a worthy cause," one commenter argued. "At the same time, immigration enforcement and whether a deportation was lawful or justified are matters for the courts and policymakers not concert stages." Fox News Digital has reached out to Musgraves' representatives for comment. Meanwhile, Musgraves stood by her remarks on social media, taking to her Instagram Story to upload a post that read, "Kinda chic when kids don't face immigration court alone." The singer also reposted a message shared by the Young Center's Instagram page, in which the organization expressed its gratitude to her. "Thank you," the nonprofit wrote. "We appreciate your support of our work and mission to see unaccompanied immigrant children safe, free, and with their families." Based in Chicago, the Young Center describes its work as pairing volunteers with attorneys and social workers to advocate for unaccompanied and separated immigrant children in government custody. Its website lists family unity, release from custody, fair proceedings and children's best interests among its priorities. The nonprofit reported serving 1,975 children from 53 countries in 2024 and opening 1,388 new cases. Its 2025 annual report said children's average detention time increased from 30 to 198 days and requests for assistance from detained parents quadrupled from 2024. Friday’s appeal extended Musgraves’ support for the charity. In April, resale platform Depop announced that 20 pieces from her wardrobe, including clothing from music videos and tours, would be sold in capsule drops. Women's Wear Daily reported that all proceeds would benefit the Young Center. In announcing the sale, Musgraves described the beneficiary without discussing immigration enforcement. "I also adore the fact that the sales are supporting a really beautiful cause," Musgraves said. Musgraves also invited three brothers, ages 18, 14 and 12, to open three Texas shows in May after their family was released from ICE custody. The mariachi performers' family said they entered through the now-defunct CBP One appointment system in 2023 and sought asylum after fleeing violence in Mexico, KSAT reported. Responding to the family’s detention, DHS said federal law required custody while its immigration claims were heard. "The law requires illegal aliens who show up at a port of entry without valid entry to be detained while all their claims are heard. You can look it up in the statute," a DHS spokesperson told KSAT. "Unlike the previous administration, the Trump administration is not going to ignore the rule of law." Musgraves' latest remarks came as ICE enforcement reached record levels. Federal sources told Fox News Digital that agents made about 51,000 immigration arrests in July, topping the previous record of roughly 43,000 in June. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "Every day, the brave men and women of ICE are arresting and DEPORTING dangerous criminal illegal aliens, including gang members, from our country," DHS said. articles.title: 'National Treasure' director predicts upcoming third film won't be able to 'ignore' politics
articles.summary: Director Jon Turteltaub said political polarization delayed "National Treasure 3" and explained the finished script will have to address modern politics.
articles.body: "National Treasure" director Jon Turteltaub suggested Friday that politics was a factor in delaying the third film in the Nicolas Cage-led franchise and predicted the issue would be addressed in the new sequel. During a live recording of the "National Treasure Hunt" podcast in Philadelphia, Turteltaub confirmed to an audience that "National Treasure 3" was "finally real" with a finished script approved by him and Disney. The original film, "National Treasure," came out in 2004 with its sequel, "National Treasure: Book of Secrets," premiering three years later in 2007. Both were directed by Turteltaub. 16 PATRIOTIC MOVIES TO WATCH THIS FOURTH OF JULY, FROM 'TOP GUN' TO 'SAVING PRIVATE RYAN' While discussing the gap between the second and third films, Turteltaub said that the growing political climate in the country made it difficult to keep working on the historical fiction film series, citing an interaction with former Republican House Speaker Kevin McCarthy. "He, like others, were surprised that Democrats made that movie because Democrats can’t be patriots," Turteltaub said, according to The Philadelphia Inquirer. "That’s the thought and it just got worse. And on the Democrats’ side: ‘Oh, Republicans, they just want to keep stuff to themselves, they hate everybody, they want to kill everyone, and blah blah blah.'" Though he did not offer many details about the third film, Turteltaub predicted that it would inevitably have to address modern politics. "We have to be very careful, but I don’t feel we are allowed to ignore it," Turteltaub said. "I think we have to include that idea in the story somehow without making someone feel put off." KELSEY GRAMMER ADMITS IT'S 'EXHAUSTING' WHEN MOVIES TRY TO ALTER HISTORY TO FIT MODERN TASTES Fox News Digital reached out to Disney for comment but did not immediately receive a response.  Turteltaub and producer Jerry Bruckheimer have hinted at the production of a third film starring Cage for years, though production has yet to take place. Even on the podcast, Turteltaub joked "things could happen" in the meantime. "Now, it’s Hollywood real, meaning things could happen. Nic gets hit by a bus, there’s no 'National Treasure 3.' If I get hit by a bus, there’s probably a 'National Treasure 3.' Welcome to Hollywood," Turteltaub said. In a comment to Fox News Digital, film critic Christian Toto, the founder and editor of Hollywood in Toto, said that it made sense for Hollywood to tackle another older franchise for nostalgia but expressed disappointment in the idea of addressing politics. DISNEY'S POLITICAL FIGHT WITH RON DESANTIS COST COMPANY YEARS OF THEME PARK EXPANSION, COURT RECORDS REVEAL "It sounds like Turteltaub, a veteran Hollywood director who isn't known for his political views, was accurately assessing how Hollywood views patriotism and the political divide," Toto said. "It's actually a sad sign of the times — a franchise about U.S. history is now seen as problematic or challenging, when it should be nothing of the kind." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "A franchise like this would be best served staying apolitical, and the director's comments suggest a way to thread the needle between acknowledging our political chasm and moving forward with a fresh new story," he added. "Heck, if that delicate balance works, it might be the biggest film in the franchise."
